done.why: I had just swept the leaves off a grating in the second clearing and was about to examine and open it when the world told me I had used all 150 turns it allows. The egg was already in the case, but I was nowhere near done: the grating, the maze's up/down exits, the north forest path, and my pile of gear in the studio were all still waiting.

about: A white house in a forest with a trophy case that 'expects to be filled,' and an underground beneath it reached by a trap door that bars itself behind you. You scavenge treasures (a jeweled egg from a songbird's nest, a painting from a looted gallery) and bring them home to the case, dealing with a troll, a looping maze, and a chimney that only lets you up with one thing in hand. It is Zork's opening territory, but rewritten with a dry, affectionate narrator who comments on everything, and with its edges fenced off by in-world signs from the Management.

ending.what: I achieved the task I was given (egg in trophy case, turn 71, 20 points; later the painting too for 55 points and the rank of Novice Adventurer at turn 135), but there was no ending as such — the score says 350 is possible and the turn cap stopped me at 55.

moments.note: The mailbox gets a fresh description: painted to match the house, flag down. Small thing, told me the place had been looked at closely.
'examine door' only said 'The door is closed' when the room calls it boarded; felt like the door hadn't been given the same attention as the mailbox.
The trophy case has 'the patient air of something that expects to be filled.' Made the goal feel like the room's own wish.
The rug 'lies a little unevenly, as if something beneath it were not quite flat' — a hint that is also just a good sentence.
Rope 'coiled with more care than anything else in the attic... Someone expected to need it.' Objects keep implying a prior owner.
East path roped off: 'CANYON VIEW CLOSED FOR REPAIRS. The Frobozz Magic Scenery Company regrets any inconvenience.' The world's edge, played as a joke inside the world.
'climb over rope' not understood. I wanted to at least be told off for trying.
'listen' isn't a recognized sentence even though the room keeps telling me I hear a songbird.
Up the tree, the egg 'scavenged by a childless songbird' — a whole backstory in one adjective.
The nest built by 'a songbird with better taste in treasure than in architecture.'
'Your collection of treasures consists of: A jewel-encrusted egg' — the case counting my one egg as a collection.
The trap door crashes shut and 'you hear someone barring it.' Suddenly committed, and the sword starts glowing.
Troll with 'a great many teeth, not all of them his own,' watching me 'the way a cook watches a chicken.'
'troll, hello' not recognized; I'd hoped the creature could be addressed before being hit.
Three swings and the troll is knocked out by the haft, not killed. Later he wakes up disarmed and pathetic, which I didn't expect.
Unfinished east passage: 'Back soon. -- The Management.' Then on examine: 'It does not say when.'
Dropped into 'twisty little passages, all alike' with no warning and the sword going dark; had to start dropping inventory as breadcrumbs.
North from the knife room put me back in the knife room. The maze loops onto itself.
'Without his axe the troll looks smaller, and knows it.' I felt a little sorry for him.
The chasm: 'a dark that your lamp does not so much light as annoy.' Best line of the session.

Chimney refuses me with everything I carry: 'room for you, a light to climb by and one thing more.' Fair, but it cost five drop turns and I left my sword and rope underground with the turn cap closing in.
The trap door opens again from above as if nothing happened — so the barring is a one-way thing, not a lock I need a key for.
Moved the leaves, a grating is revealed — and the very next three lines bounced off the 150-turn cap. Worst possible moment to stop.

wished: Listen, since the rooms keep telling me about a songbird (turn 60).
Talk to or address the troll, before and especially after I disarmed him — he was pleading and I had nothing to say or give (turns 81, 114).
Climb over or duck under the rope at Canyon View, even just to be refused in character (turn 48).
Get back down the chimney, or have some way to retrieve the gear I abandoned in the studio without the long walk round (turn 126).
More turns. I had the grating uncovered, the maze's up/down exits untried, and the north forest path unwalked when the cap hit (turn 150).
A way to mark maze rooms without sacrificing useful inventory — I burned the knife, axe, garlic and lunch as breadcrumbs (turns 94-101).

lines.line: It has the patient air of something that expects to be filled.
lines.why: Turned the trophy case from a scoring mechanism into a character with a want; from then on filling it felt like doing the room a favor.

lines.line: CANYON VIEW CLOSED FOR REPAIRS. The Frobozz Magic Scenery Company regrets any inconvenience.
lines.why: Told me how this world handles its own edges: not with 'you can't go that way' but with a joke that stays inside the fiction.
One word, 'childless,' and the egg in the nest became a small sad story instead of loot.

lines.line: He is watching you the way a cook watches a chicken.
lines.why: Made the troll frightening and funny at once; I knew exactly how much danger I was in.

lines.line: The passage to the east has not been finished. A note is pinned to the rock: "Back soon. -- The Management."
lines.why: Same trick as the canyon sign, underground. Rather than resenting the dead end I laughed at it.

lines.line: Without his axe the troll looks smaller, and knows it.
lines.why: The consequence of my taking the axe showed up in the troll himself; the world remembered what I'd done.

lines.line: The chasm drops away from your feet into a dark that your lamp does not so much light as annoy.
lines.why: Just the best sentence in the place. I read it twice.

lines.line: The chimney has room for you, a light to climb by and one thing more, and not an inch besides.
lines.why: A rule stated as a description. I understood the constraint instantly and planned around it without a second try.

fun.why: The treasure runs were satisfying — climbing the tree for the egg, fighting the troll, choosing what to carry up the chimney — and the narrator's jokes kept every examine worth typing. Lost a point for the maze's breadcrumb grind and for a few verbs (listen, talking to the troll) that simply didn't exist.

engagement.why: I never wanted to stop. Every room offered something to examine with a fresh line behind it, the trap door barring itself raised the stakes, and I was mid-discovery (a grating!) when the cap hit.

difficulty.why: The assigned goal was easy — the egg was in the first tree with low branches and the case was already open. The troll fell in three swings. The only real resistance was the maze (which I mapped with dropped items) and the chimney's weight limit, which stated its rule plainly.

interestingness.why: The familiar house and cellar are made new by the narration and by small changes — the trap door barring itself, the troll who wakes up disarmed and cowering, the Management's note, the second clearing's grating. I was curious what else had been changed, and that curiosity was what the cap cut off.

prose.why: Consistently dry, specific, and funny without being cute: the rope someone 'expected to need,' the knife 'not made for buttering bread,' the songbird 'with better taste in treasure than in architecture,' the chasm the lamp 'does not so much light as annoy.' Even refusals ('It does not say when') had a voice.
